newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy offers temporary shelter to Albanians.
newsitem.headline: Italy offers temporary shelter to Albanians.

text.p: Italy said on Saturday it would grant temporary shelter to Albanians fleeing chaos in their homeland as more refugees streamed across the Adriatic in a fleet of decrepit boats.

But junior interior minister Nicola Sinisi said the refugees would not be given political asylum because the crisis in Albania was a "degeneration of public order" and not war. They would be repatriated once the armed anarchy subsided.

"At this stage we have the duty for humanitarian reasons to keep people who are not able to live in their country. However, we have the duty to do this only for a limited period of time," Sinisi told reporters in the south-east port of Brindisi.
"At the end of this period, they will be repatriated. First on a voluntary basis and later through other means."
Sinisi estimated that the period of temporary sanctuary could last about three months.
Sinisi spoke after a crisis meeting of Italian security and immigration chiefs in Brindisi called in response to an influx of Albanians in rusting vessels, many of them decades-old navy patrol boats.

The Italian news agency Ansa reported that by Saturday evening, 2,703 Albanians and 91 boats had arrived in south-east Italy since insurrection began spreading through the impoverished Balkan state this month.

Sinisi said the boats would be impounded so they could not be used for further crossings. He told local officials that the region would not accommodate more than 3,000 refugees and subsequent arrivals would be moved to other areas.
Four more boats arrived in Brindisi shortly after midday, including a fishing boat with around 190 on board and another with about 75 people.
Italian coast guards said two Albanian navy ships had also been intercepted in the Adriatic, each packed with 200 to 300 people, many of them children.

One of them was idle about 10 miles off the coast and coast guards were transferring a group of about 40 women and children to navy boats and then to Brindisi. The other was further behind and being escorted by the navy.
Andrea Gentile, the chief of police in Brindisi, said the port had no shelter for more refugees.
He said there was still space for Albanian boats to enter port but those on board would have to stay there. "The reception centres are completely full," he said.
The problem of what to do with the refugees is a pressing issue for Italy, already a magnet for illegal immigrants.
Their arrival has raised fears in Italy of a repeat of the tide of 40,000 Albanians who flooded into south-east ports in 1991 after Stalinist rule crumbled in Europe's poorest state.
Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano said in Naples earlier on Saturday that Italy should brace for a huge influx.

But Sinisi said the impounding of boats already in Italy and a reported scarcity of seagoing vessels still off Albania would contain the problem. "There is no crisis situation...we don't envisage a mass exodus," he told reporters.
He said many of the Albanians who had arrived had been fingerprinted. About 150 of them were deserting servicemen and a number of prisoners who escaped jails stormed by rioters.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees urged Italy and Greece on Friday to allow Albanians fleeing the turmoil, sparked by the collapse of shady pyramid savings schemes, to enter and stay "as long as necessary".
